sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Wandjina** ​(*wandjina*) — ‌Cloud, ‌Rain Spirits ​· Ancestral ​beings ​of monsoon ​skies ​— belongs ‌to ​the Aboriginal ​tradition, where ‌it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Cloud, ​Rain Spirits". ​The name ​means ​"The cloud ​spirits"[^1].

‌**Wandjina** are ​the ‌cloud-and-rain beings ​of ‌the Kimberley ​region of ‌Western ​Australia. Painted ‌on ​rock shelter ​walls ‌with large ‌eyes, no ‌mouth, ​and radiating ​halos, ‌they are ​not ​merely art ‌but living ​ancestral ​powers who ‌control ​the monsoon, ‌punish ​wrongdoers, and ​keep the ​moral ​and ecological ‌order ‌of country.[^2]

​PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical scholarly ​spelling ‌**Wandjina** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/wandjina/). ‌The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *wandjina* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

Crawford, Ian M., The Art of the Wandjina: Aboriginal Cave Paintings in Kimberley, Western Australia.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Wandjina** ​is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken ‌form. Etymologically ​the ‌name means ​"The ‌cloud spirits"[^1].

​The ​canonical spelling ​**Wandjina** ​matches the ​conventional ‌scholarly romanization. ​The ‌plain ASCII ​form ‌*wandjina* contains ​the ‌same letters, ​so ‌no lost ​diacritics ​or encoding ‌transition ‌is ‌claimed. The ​editorial ​work is ‌to ​fix one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. ​The displayed ​form ‌is ASCII-equivalent ‌— ​a description ‌computed ​from ​the displayed ‌form ‌itself.

The ‌letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

- ​**w** ‌→ **W** ​— ​Same, capitalized
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ​Same
- **n** ​→ ‌**n** — ​Same
- ​**d** → ​**d** ‌— Same
- ​**j** ‌→ **j** ​— ‌Same
- ​**i** → ‌**i** ‌— Same
- ​**n** ​→ **n** ​— ​Same
- **a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The conventional ​reading of the name ‌is **/wɒnˈdʒiːnə/** — Worrorra/Ngarinyin ‌approximation[^1].

For the English ​speaker, the closest approximation ​is: 'won-JEE-nuh' — stress ​the middle syllable, keep ​the first vowel like ​British 'hot,' and pronounce ‌the final 'a' as ​a light open vowel.

​Wandjina is a simpler ‌restoration because the ASCII ​form *wandjina* already represents ‌the same phonemic sequence; ​no stress mark, length ‌mark, or distinctive letter ​is required to recover ​the spoken name. The ​Aboriginal laminal consonants and ​the exact vowel qualities ​of the Kimberley languages ‌are not reproducible in ​basic Latin script, but ‌the scholarly romanisation records ​the name well enough ‌for citation and discussion.

​The related forms **Wanjina** ‌(Ngarinyin/Wunambal) and **Wanjarri** preserve ​the same consonant skeleton ‌with minor spelling variation. ​In all cases, the ​middle syllable carries the ‌stress, and the name ‌names both individual ancestral ‌beings and the collective ​cloud-and-rain powers of the ​Kimberley.

Because Wandjina belongs ‌to an oral tradition, ​the reconstructed pronunciation offered ​here is a scholarly ‌romanization rather than a ​phonetic record of a ​living speaker. The sounds ‌of the original language ​include phonemes that English ‌does not distinguish, and ​early recorders used inconsistent ​English-based spellings. PuniCodex therefore ​treats the capitalized scholarly ​form **Wandjina** as the ‌reference spelling, while noting ‌that the ASCII form ​represents the same romanized ‌sequence. This is why ​the name is classified ​as a plain restoration: ‌the restoration recovers the ‌proper-noun convention of the ‌name without adding a ‌diacritic or special letter ​that the original ASCII ‌string could not carry.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous writing ‌system is ‌securely attested ​for individual ​aboriginal names. ​The form ​shown ​is a ‌modern scholarly ​transliteration.[^1]

The ​form **Wandjina** ‌is therefore ​a scholarly ‌transliteration ​rather than ‌an attested ​ancient spelling; ​it encodes ​the reconstructed ​sound ​of the ‌name for ​modern use, ‌and no ​mark in ‌it is ​decorative.

‌The Aboriginal ​languages of ‌the Kimberley ​were not ​written in ‌a European ‌sense ‌before colonisation. ​The name ​is known ‌orally in ​Worrorra, Ngarinyin, ​and Wunambal ‌forms ​and was ​first rendered ‌in Latin ​script by ‌anthropologists and ​linguists ​in the ​twentieth century. ​The spelling ‌'Wandjina' follows ‌the conventional ​scholarly romanisation ‌used ​by AIATSIS ​and by ‌researchers such ‌as Ian ‌Crawford. Because ‌the distinctive ​sounds ‌and semantic ​fields of ​the original ​languages cannot ‌be conveyed ​by basic ​Latin ​letters alone, ‌and because ​the restoration ​does not ​add diacritics ‌or ​special letters, ‌the name ​is classified ‌as a ​plain restoration. ‌The canonical ‌form ​remains the ​scholarly citation ​form; the ​ASCII form ‌is a ‌lowercase ASCII ​equivalent.

sources.citation: Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies, Canberra, 1964.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Wandjina are ​first of ‌all the ‌powers of ​**cloud, rain, ​and storm**. ​Their eyes ​are said ​to be ‌the source ​of lightning; ​their halos ‌are the ​clouds and ‌storm light ​of the ‌wet season; ​their anger ​is thunder ​and destructive ​cyclone. They ​control the ‌monsoon that ​replenishes the ‌waterholes, rivers, ​and coastal ‌plains of ​the Kimberley ‌after the ​long dry.

Beyond ‌weather, they ​are the ​**owners and ‌managers of ‌country**. Each ‌Wandjina is ​associated with ​specific clan ‌estates, sacred ​sites, and ​stretches of ‌the ancestral ​journey across ​the Kimberley. ‌They gave ​the Law ‌that governs ​kinship, marriage, ​food restrictions, ​fire management, ​and the ‌proper treatment ‌of sacred ​places.

They ‌are also ​**figures of ​restricted knowledge**. ‌The right ‌to paint, ‌name, and speak ‌for a ​Wandjina belongs ‌to senior ​initiated custodians. ​The images ​are refreshed ‌rather than ​replaced, and ​their reproduction ​is controlled ‌by cultural ​protocol. This ​means that ​the Wandjina ‌domain is ​not only ‌meteorological or ​territorial but ‌also juridical: ​they embody ‌the authority ‌through which ​Aboriginal people ​of the ​Kimberley maintain ​their relationship ‌to land ‌and to ​one another[^3].

Crawford, Ian M., The Art of the Wandjina: Aboriginal Cave Paintings in Kimberley, Western Australia.
Mowaljarlai, David, and Jutta Malnic, Yorro Yorro: Everything Standing Up Alive.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
- ​**Large ‌eyes** ‌— ​The ​source ​of lightning; ​the ​all-seeing ‌gaze ​of ​the ‌ancestors.
- ​**Absence ‌of ​mouth** ‌— ​A ​sign ​of sacred ​reticence; ​the ‌Wandjina ​do ‌not ​speak ‌casually, ​and ‌their ​power ‌is ​enacted rather ​than ‌narrated.
- ‌**Radiating ‌halo** ​— ​Clouds, ‌storm ​light, ​and ‌the ​luminescence ​of ‌the wet-season ​sky.
- ‌**Rock ​shelter** ​— ​The ​gallery ‌walls ‌where ​the ‌Wandjina ​retreated ​after ‌bestowing Law, ‌leaving ‌their ‌images ​as ‌witnesses.
- ​**Rainbow ​serpent** ​— ‌A ​related ​power ​of water ‌and ​transformation, ​sometimes ​associated ‌with ​the ‌same ​sacred ‌geography.
- ​**Waterhole ‌and ‌river** ​— The ​country ​the ​Wandjina ‌replenish ‌and ​protect.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Wandjina cosmology ​is not a ‌single linear narrative ‌but a body ​of law carried ​by clan estates, ​initiation sequences, and ​painted galleries. The ​common thread is ‌that the Wandjina came ​from the sea ​and the sky, ‌shaped the country, ​gave Law to ‌the people, and ​then returned to ‌the rock walls, ​where their images ​remain as living ​presences.

In one ​widespread account, the ​Wandjina travelled across ‌the Kimberley in ​the ancestral past, ‌creating the hills, ​rivers, waterholes, and ‌species that define the ​country. Each clan ‌holds the part ​of the journey ‌that passes through ​its estate; the ​full map of ‌their travels is ‌known only through ‌the combined authority ​of many custodians. ​When their work ‌was complete, they ​lay down on ​the rock-shelter walls ‌and left their ​images behind, yet ​they remain present ‌in cloud and rain.

​The giving of ‌Law is central ​to the tradition. ​The Wandjina established ​the rules governing ​kinship, marriage, food ‌restrictions, fire management, ‌and the treatment ​of sacred sites. ‌This Law is ​not static scripture ​but a living ‌obligation transmitted through ‌initiation, story, and ‌country.

As the ‌build-up gives way ​to the monsoon, ‌the Wandjina are understood ​to be active ​in the thunderheads ​and lightning that ‌cross the coast. ​Their anger can ​bring destructive cyclones; ​their blessing brings ‌the rain that ​fills the waterholes ​and revives the ​country after the ‌long dry.

Wandjina ​paintings are periodically ‌refreshed by those ​authorised to do ‌so. A faded ​image is not abandoned; ‌it is a ‌spirit in need ​of care. The ​act of repainting ​is a renewal ​of the relationship ‌between the custodians, ‌the ancestors, and ​the country[^3].

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Wandjina ​belief has ‌never ‌been a ​unified 'religion' ​in ​the colonial ​sense; ​it is ‌a regional ​complex ​shared across ‌linguistically ​distinct peoples ‌of ​the Kimberley, ‌including the ​Worrora, ​Ngarinyin, and ​Wunambal. ​Each group ​holds ‌its own ​portion of ‌the ​total tradition, ‌and ​knowledge is ‌stratified by ​age, ‌gender, and ​initiation ​status. In ‌the ‌late twentieth ‌century, artists ​such ​as David ‌Mowaljarlai ​and other ​Kimberley ‌elders began ​to explain ​Wandjina ‌significance to ​wider ‌Australian and ​international audiences, ​not ​as a ​syncretic ‌new movement ‌but ​as a ‌deliberate act ​of ​cultural translation ‌on ‌their own ‌terms. ‌The Wandjina ​have also ‌entered ​Australian popular ​culture, ​sometimes without ‌permission, prompting ​ongoing ​debates about ​copyright, ‌cultural heritage, ​and ​the right ​of traditional ‌owners ​to control ‌sacred ​imagery.[^1]

Within ‌the ​Aboriginal tradition, ‌closely related ‌names ​in the ​corpus ​include [[altjira|Altjira]], ​[[baiame|Baiame]], [[bunjil|Bunjil]], ‌[[daramulum|Daramulum]], ‌[[eingana|Eingana]], and ​[[gnowee|Gnowee]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
The Wandjina ​are among the ‌most recognisable and culturally ‌significant rock-art traditions ​in Australia. Their ​galleries in the ​Kimberley, including sites on ​the Mitchell Plateau ​and along the ‌Gibb River Road, ​are visited under strict ​protocols and are ‌sometimes closed to ​the public. The ‌images have shaped Australian ​understandings of Indigenous ‌art, cosmology, and ​land tenure, and ​they continue to be ​a focus of ​heritage management, repatriation ​discussions, and Aboriginal ‌self-determination. Contemporary Kimberley artists ​work within and ‌against this legacy, ​producing new art ‌that honours ancestral authority ​while addressing modern ‌audiences[^3].

Today Wandjina ​appears in Aboriginal ‌Australian art, storytelling, environmental ​education, and cultural ​tourism, always under ‌the guidance of ‌the communities who hold ‌the name. Bark ​paintings, rock-art sites, ​dance cycles, and ‌welcome-to-country ceremonies keep the ​figure present in ​public life, while ‌restricted knowledge remains ​within appropriate kin and ​ceremonial contexts. The ‌name also serves ​as a reminder ‌that the domain-name system ​was built on ​ASCII assumptions that ​erase the proper-noun ​conventions of many Indigenous ‌languages; restoring **Wandjina** ‌as a flagship ​temple is one ‌small act of acknowledging ​that erasure and ​preserving the scholarly ‌citation form for ‌future reference.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
The ​Wandjina ask ‌us ‌to think ​about ​power differently. ​They ​are not ​remote ‌gods in ​a ​heaven separate ‌from ​earth; they ‌are ​in the ‌clouds, ​the lightning, ​the ​rock shelters, ​and ​the Law. ‌Their ​images do ‌not ​'represent' them ‌the ​way a ‌portrait ​represents a ‌person; ​the image ​is ‌a site ‌of ‌presence, a ​place ​where the ‌ancestral ​power continues ​to ‌act.

This ​is ​why the ‌question ​of who ‌may ​paint, photograph, ​or ​reproduce a ​Wandjina ‌is not ‌merely ​a matter ‌of ​copyright. It ​is ‌a question ‌of ‌who holds ‌the ​relationship. In ‌a ​world that ​treats ​images as ‌endlessly ​reproducible content, ​the ​Wandjina stand ‌as ​a reminder ​that ​some images ‌are ​obligations, not ‌assets. ​To speak ‌their ​name respectfully ‌is ‌to acknowledge ​the ​country, the ​custodians, ​and the ‌living ‌Law they ​protect.[^1]
